chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ibn Abi 'Umayr from al-Husayn ibn 'Uthman from whom he mentioned from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who gives the zakat of his wealth to a man while he believes him to be insolvent (poor), but then finds him to be wealthy (able to pay), he said: 'It does not count (is not valid) for him.'

key_terms.لاَ يُجْزِي: It does not count / is not valid
key_terms.مُعْسِرٌ: Insolvent or poor (one who cannot pay debts)
key_terms.مُوسِراً: Wealthy or able to pay (one who has means)

ai.seo_question: Does zakat count if given to someone who turns out to be rich?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Tusi's *Tahdhib* clarifies the condition of 'ignorance of status' (jahil) in zakat validity, a key point of discussion among Shia jurists regarding whether the recipient's actual state at the time of payment or the giver's belief at the time of distribution determines validity. It underscores the principle that zakat is a specific act of worship requiring precise fulfillment of its conditions, meaning if the core requirement of poverty is absent, the obligation is not discharged. This ruling highlights the meticulous attention Shia fiqh pays to the internal and external conditions of charitable obligations.
